overview: The atlas drops you into a steppe world just after a political earthquake. Its single 1400 polygon calls the western Jochid lands “Blue Horde,” stretching from Crimea and the lower Volga far enough to swallow Moscow on the screen. Medieval names are less obedient: some modern histories call the western wing Blue and the eastern White, while a study of documents made inside the Jochid realm reverses those colors. So this card follows people and institutions, not paint. Tokhtamysh had reunited the wings before Timur smashed his power in 1395. Then rival Chinggisid khans, the formidable emir Edigü, city officials, merchants, herders and diplomats kept the realm working while it fragmented. Sarai, Astrakhan, Crimea, pasture routes and river crossings linked mobile camps with mosques, mints, workshops and markets. You will meet felt-covered wagon homes, millet-and-milk dishes, silver coins carrying Arabic words, elite women with property, children’s whistles and ankle-bone games, bathhouses, and very patchy toilet evidence. By the 1430s and 1440s, Kazan, Crimea, the Great Horde, Astrakhan and Nogai power were taking distinct paths. The atlas swaps Blue Horde for Golden Horde in 1492; history did not click over that neatly, and Jochid communities did not vanish.

periods.title: Batu’s western inheritance becomes a connected Jochid realm
periods.summary: Batu’s branch led the western or Right Wing from the lower Volga. Sarai, steppe pastures, Rus tribute relations and Black Sea routes belonged to one Jochid political world, although later color labels do not stay consistent.

periods.title: The senior line breaks and rivals crowd the throne
periods.summary: After Berdibeg’s death, competing Chinggisid claimants and powerful emirs fought for Sarai. Political rivalry disrupted communities and trade, while the Chinggisid rule that only Jochi’s descendants could be khan still shaped every coalition.

periods.title: Tokhtamysh reunites the wings, then loses to Timur
periods.summary: Tokhtamysh reunited eastern and western Jochid power, then quarreled with Timur. Timur’s 1395 campaign shattered Tokhtamysh’s position and damaged the political center just before the atlas begins its Blue Horde display.

periods.title: The map’s predecessor cracks before its color split
periods.summary: Tokhtamysh remained a claimant after 1395, but Edigü and rival Chinggisids contested the realm. The atlas still draws one broad Golden Horde predecessor until 1400, hiding the struggle already under way.

periods.title: Edigü and rival khans dominate the first atlas phase
periods.summary: The western steppe did not become one new Blue Horde in 1400. Edigü exercised enormous power while installing or opposing Chinggisid khans, and Tokhtamysh’s family continued seeking allies and the throne.

periods.title: Ulugh Muhammad writes from a contested Golden Horde
periods.summary: Ulugh Muhammad alternately held and lost Sarai while Barak, Dawlat Birdi and other rivals controlled different regions. His 1428 letter shows diplomacy and trade continuing inside a fractured political landscape.

periods.title: Successor khanates and the Great Horde take separate paths
periods.summary: Kazan, Crimea, Astrakhan, Nogai power and the Great Horde emerged from Jochid regional bases. Ahmad’s 1480 Ugra withdrawal was important, but the Great Horde and other Jochid polities outlived it.

periods.title: The atlas renames the remnant before its documented end
periods.summary: At 1492 the Blue Horde id becomes a smaller golden-horde feature. The Great Horde continued beyond that seam until 1502, while Crimean, Kazan, Astrakhan, Nogai and Siberian lines carried Jochid institutions forward.

sections.title: Audit the painted horde before trusting it

items.text: The exact live target is blue-horde, displayed “Blue Horde,” aliased “Golden Horde,” and indexed circa 1400 to 1492. Coverage records one border file and no card or override before this packet. Those database facts establish what must be documented; they do not prove that people in 1400 called their government Blue Horde.

In the 1300 snapshot, blue-horde does not exist. One broad khanate-of-the-golden-horde polygon covers tested places from Crimea and Sarai east toward Orenburg and Mangystau; a second feature with that same id carries the label Ryazan. The 1400 color split is therefore an atlas redraw, not a witnessed founding event.

At 1400 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 193 positions. Its bounds are about 29.12° to 50.21° east and 42.44° to 62.21° north. Point tests place Sarai, Astrakhan, Crimea and Azov inside, while Kyiv, Kazan, Bolgar, Orenburg, Oral, Sighnaq and Mangystau fall outside.

The same ring also contains tested Moscow, even though Moscow was a Rus principality negotiating tribute, patents and war with Jochid rulers, not an ordinary patch of directly administered steppe. Meanwhile Kazan and Bolgar fall in the separate white-horde shape. That mismatch makes the polygon a locator, not a surveyed frontier.

At 1492 blue-horde vanishes. A smaller golden-horde feature contains Sarai, Astrakhan, Kazan, Bolgar and Oral; Ottoman geometry contains Crimea and Azov; Muscovy contains Moscow. Golden-horde persists with changed geometry at 1500, then later Nogai, Kazan and Sibir ids appear. This is a layered handoff, not one clean fall.

The atlas follows a familiar modern convention: Blue Horde in the western steppe and White Horde in the east. Its two 1400 polygons prove how this dataset applies the colors. They cannot decide what a Persian chronicler, a Turkic chancery or a later Russian historian meant by the same words.

A study centered on sources produced inside the Jochid world finds the opposite late-fourteenth-century usage: the western Right Wing, or sometimes the whole realm, could be Aq Orda, White Horde, while the eastern Left Wing could be Kök Orda, Blue Horde. Both arrangements appear in modern scholarship, so neither color is timeless.

The safest identity for this card is “the western Jochid or Golden Horde succession zone represented by the atlas’s Blue Horde polygon.” It follows the map without inventing a stable self-name. The color label works like a library shelf: useful for finding the story, dangerous if mistaken for a medieval passport stamp.

The index keeps khanate-of-the-golden-horde, blue-horde, white-horde and golden-horde as separate ids at successive seams. At 1530 it adds Nogai, Kazan and Sibir. It has no medieval Uzbek, Great Horde, Crimean or Astrakhan id; only modern Uzbekistan appears. This card names those historical polities without pretending every one has its own map record.

Evidence is lopsided. Rus chronicles, Persian histories, Arabic geographies, Italian records, coins and a few Jochid letters illuminate different places and agendas. Elite succession is far easier to see than an ordinary child’s day. Whenever this card reaches from wider Golden Horde evidence toward the exact western polygon, it says so.

sections.title: How the western wing was built, united and broken

items.text: Jochi, eldest son of Chinggis Khan, died before his father. Jochi’s sons inherited a vast western realm: Batu’s line led the western or Right Wing, while Orda’s line held an eastern or Left Wing. The wings belonged to one political family even when their rulers managed different territories and later writers swapped their colors.

Sarai on the lower Volga became an administrative center, but the realm was never only a city-state. UNESCO’s Bolgar evidence shows towns, mosques, bathhouses and workshops interacting with mobile steppe communities and long-distance routes. Pasture and pavement belonged to the same economy, even when rulers preferred a tented court.

Muslim influence grew over generations; Berke was Muslim, and the khans from Özbeg onward were Muslim. Islam linked rulers, judges, scholars, merchants and builders across Eurasia, while conversion and practice remained uneven among regions and households. A ruler’s faith did not turn every subject into one language, ancestry or daily routine.

Berdibeg’s murder in 1359 ended the senior Batuid line and opened a long struggle. Rival royal descendants needed emirs, regional troops and supplies; emirs still needed a Chinggisid prince to be khan. Communities faced more than palace drama, because fighting and divided authority could disrupt food, travel, tribute and trade.

Tokhtamysh reunited the major Jochid wings around 1378, then fought the Timur who had first helped him. Timur’s 1395 invasion wrecked Tokhtamysh’s bid to rule the whole realm. The atlas begins its Blue Horde in 1400, after this earthquake, so its start date cannot be the founding of an unchanged western state.

sections.title: Edigü, rival khans and government by coalition

items.text: Edigü was a Manghit emir, not a Chinggisid khan. He could command armies, arrange alliances and elevate or abandon royal claimants, yet he usually ruled through descendants of Jochi because Chinggisid ancestry still supplied legitimate khans. His career shows that a title and practical power could sit on different saddles.

After Tokhtamysh’s defeat, Tokhtamysh and his sons kept seeking the throne while Edigü and his allies resisted them. Lithuania, Rus principalities and neighboring rulers could shelter claimants or become allies and targets. Diplomacy was therefore part of warfare: a prince needed messengers and marriages as much as fast horses.

A khan’s authority traveled through regional yurts, emirs, tax collectors, judges, city officials and commanders rather than through a neat modern border service. The two-wing system could coordinate enormous space, but local power brokers mattered. That flexibility helped government survive travel distances; it also let coalitions fragment when the center weakened.

War did not erase every institution each time the throne changed. Bolgar’s layers preserve continued trade, worship, craft activity, baths and building across Volga Bulgar, Golden Horde and Kazan phases. The site warns against a drumbeat history in which rulers fight while towns vanish between paragraphs; people repaired, traded and adapted.

Written authority helped a traveling court govern: bitikchi prepared documents in Turkic and Mongolian using the Uyghur script, while multilingual borderlands needed mediation. Orders and credentials could move farther than one official. That system connected rulers, commanders and cities, but surviving court papers reveal little about ordinary households.

sections.title: From Ulugh Muhammad to a family of successor states

items.text: Ulugh Muhammad became a major khan after Edigü’s death but repeatedly lost and regained power. Barak, Dawlat Birdi and other Jochids controlled rival regions. His March 1428 letter says he had driven off Barak and Mansur and recovered throne and realm, which is a claimant’s political statement, not a neutral census.

The same letter asks to restore good relations with Ottoman Murad II through envoys, gifts, greetings and ortaq merchants traveling by land and water. It shows that fractured rule did not stop diplomacy or trade. It also shows a khan advertising security: safe merchants made useful proof that his authority worked.

By the middle decades of the fifteenth century, regional Jochid projects became more distinct: Kazan on the upper Volga, Crimea by the Black Sea, the Great Horde around the lower Volga, Astrakhan, and Manghit or Nogai power east of it. Eastern Abu’l-Khayrid Uzbeks belong to the separate White Horde story, not this western card.

Crimea followed its own diplomatic path under the Girays, balancing Poland-Lithuania, the Great Horde, Genoese colonies and the expanding Ottoman sphere. Ottoman intervention in 1475 changed Black Sea power, but it did not make every inland Jochid polity Ottoman. The atlas’s broad Blue Horde quietly hides these different relationships.

Ahmad Khan’s 1480 campaign ended in a tense stand across the Ugra. Polish-Lithuanian help did not arrive, conditions worsened and Ahmad withdrew. Later Russian tradition made this a clean liberation date, while other accounts explain the retreat differently. It weakened Great Horde claims over Moscow; it did not end every Jochid state.

sections.title: Herds, markets, coins and moving information

items.text: Pastoral families turned grass and water into transport, meat, milk, hides, wool and animals for exchange. Seasonal movement required route knowledge, shared labor and decisions about pasture; it was planned work, not random wandering. Town markets depended on these producers, while camps depended on grain, metalwork and other urban goods.

Bolgar’s archaeology preserves a fortified urban plan, mosque, mausoleums, khanly buildings, bathhouses and craft areas. Those discoveries show major engineering and specialized labor inside the wider Jochid economy. They do not mean everyone lived in brick: wooden houses, mobile dwellings and temporary camps remained equally real parts of the landscape.

Northern trade routes drew Byzantine, Italian, Armenian and other merchants into Dasht-i Qipchaq. Goods, money, news and diplomatic letters moved together. Conflict could interrupt a route, but rulers also courted merchants because tolls, supplies and prestige followed them. The Silk Road here was a network of river ports, tracks and bargains.

Ulugh Muhammad’s coinage appeared at Hajji Tarkhan, Ordu Bazar, Sarai and Caffa. At Caffa, small silver pieces combined a Genoese-facing Latin design with an Arabic royal legend and a Jochid tamgha. That compact object records negotiation among a khan, an Italian colony, Islamic titles and Black Sea commerce.

Coins, charters, bath heating, aqueducts and craft workshops are achievements, but none belongs to one ethnicity alone. Jochid cities gathered builders, merchants and scribes from many traditions. The most impressive technology may have been coordination: making pasture routes, ports, markets, taxes and written orders connect over enormous distances.

sections.title: Families, ranks, women, children and learning

items.text: Rank shaped opportunity. Khans and royal families stood at the top; emirs and begs could command powerful coalitions. Court officials, merchants, attendants and servants filled other positions, while enslaved people endured coercion. These were overlapping relationships, not a tidy five-step social ladder.

Kinship mattered in royal succession and households sharing herding, travel and craft work, but family records are scarce. Archaeology reveals rooms, sleeping platforms and children’s objects more readily than affection, quarrels or household size. This card avoids inventing a standard Blue Horde family with fixed roles.

Ibn Battuta saw elite Golden Horde women holding property and receiving public respect, with their own large traveling households. Those households also included servants and enslaved girls. His court visit predates 1400 and describes princesses, so it proves female political and material power at the top, not equality for every woman.

Children appear in burials, changing family sleeping platforms and a child-associated room at Sarai, but records are uneven and mortality was high. Small finds return children to imperial history without pretending we know their names. A broken toy can say “a child was here” when chronicles notice only khans.

Some boys in selected urban or elite families could train for religious, commercial or chancery literacy; bitikchi scribes needed languages and the Uyghur script. Most children’s learning is harder to document. Herding, cooking, sewing and crafts were probably learned through participation, but no surviving Blue Horde timetable says who learned what.

sections.title: Homes, meals, clothes, work and play

items.text: Ibn Battuta described felt-covered wagon homes drawn by animals in the wider Golden Horde. A mobile home protected belongings and let an elite household travel with a court; simpler pastoral families had fewer resources. The account is earlier and court-centered, but it makes one point vividly: sometimes moving house meant moving the house.

The traveler also reported millet porridge mixed with mare’s milk, meat and a pasta-like dish cooked with milk. This is a valuable fourteenth-century food snapshot, not a menu for every 1400s table. Season, herd mix, wealth, farming access, religion and whether someone lived in camp or town all changed a meal.

Steppe crafts supplied clothing, shoes, tools, weapons and horse gear, while imported silk, fine textiles, jewelry and prestigious arms marked wealth. Sources assign some textile work to women and some wood or metal work to men, but those reports do not create universal job rules. Felt, leather, wool and silk told different economic stories.

Work crossed the camp-town divide: tending animals, repairing tack, processing dairy, farming, carrying water, firing ceramics, smithing, building and trading all supported one another. Captive trading was also profitable for some rulers and merchants, which makes the network’s darker truth unavoidable: somebody’s market success could begin with another family’s violent separation.

Golden Horde archaeology includes whistles, tiny dishes, animal figurines, balls and sheep or goat ankle bones used in games. Not every object can be tied to a child or the exact Blue Horde polygon, yet the collection makes daily life less silent. Even a future emir probably lost an astragalus under the furniture.

sections.title: Islam, scholarship and words struck in silver

items.text: Islam was central to Jochid court titles, law, diplomacy and urban building by the atlas period, but Islamisation was a process rather than a switch. Traveling scholars and texts connected the Golden Horde with Anatolia and other Muslim regions. Older local traditions and different Christian, Jewish and other communities also remained present.

Bolgar’s mosque, mausoleums and pilgrimage memory show religious continuity; baths joined bodily care with Islamic ablution in towns. A monument proves trained builders and patrons invested in a place. It cannot reveal how often every herder prayed, what every household believed or whether each child entered a school.

Golden Horde government used specialist scribes called bitikchi. Repository research says they needed Mongolian and Turkic and the Uyghur script; other diplomatic settings also demanded Arabic, Persian, Latin or Slavic mediation. Multilingual paperwork was a political technology. Its survival does not imply that most people could read it.

Ulugh Muhammad’s original 1428 letter survives in the Topkapı archive with five seal impressions. Its Turkic text asks for envoys, gifts and merchant movement and dates itself to 14 March beside the Dnieper. It is precious precisely because so few original western Jochid documents survive; court prose cannot stand in for home speech.

A securely period-tied Caffa coin reads **السلطان العادل محمد خان**. Transliteration: **al-sulṭān al-ʿādil Muḥammad Khān**. Translation: **“The just sultan, Muhammad Khan.”** The silver issues date about 1421 to 1435. This is normalized Unicode for an Arabic die legend, not a facsimile; real 15 to 17 mm coins are cramped, worn and sometimes incomplete.

sections.title: Medicine, water, baths, toilets and what continued

items.text: Arabic writers reported mineral springs visited for chronic illness, and a modern study argues that water treatments and baths formed part of Golden Horde healing practice. This supports “people tried hydrotherapy,” not “the spring cured them.” Evidence for household herbs, surgery, childbirth care and veterinary medicine in the exact polygon remains too thin for confident recipes.

Bolgar’s nomination records fountains, aqueducts and open water containers alongside a public bath. These discoveries demonstrate planned urban water handling, but their dates and uses vary. People in mobile camps instead depended on rivers, springs and wells along routes. Neither setting guarantees clean water by modern standards or equal access.

Archaeologists had identified 25 Golden Horde bathhouses in the cited survey: 14 communal and 11 private. Heated rooms and water management were substantial urban technologies, and bathing also served Islamic ablution. The count spans the wider Golden Horde and several periods, so it is evidence for a city tradition, not one bath per Blue Horde neighborhood.

Toilet evidence is thinner than bath evidence. A childhood study discusses potties and urinal tubes in cradle reconstructions, but provenience varies; no chosen source establishes a standard adult latrine or camp waste system for 1400 to 1492. Aqueducts are not automatically sewers. The honest bathroom answer is mostly “we do not know.”

The atlas ends Blue Horde in 1492, yet the western Jochid story continued. The replacement golden-horde feature, Great Horde until 1502, and Crimean, Kazan, Astrakhan, Nogai and Siberian successors carried forward dynasties, Islam, languages, trade skills and communities. A map label disappeared; families and political traditions did not.

ending.text: The 1492 endpoint is an atlas identifier seam. Western Jochid power had already branched into the Great Horde, Crimea, Kazan, Astrakhan and Nogai networks, and the Great Horde itself survived until 1502. Descendant communities, Islamic institutions, Turkic literary traditions, trade routes and Chinggisid political memory continued far beyond either date.
